edges.effect_quant: In the 2016 general-population meta-analysis, resting heart rate above 80 beats per minute carried a relative risk of 1.45 for all-cause mortality versus the lowest category. The broader 2017 dose-response meta-analysis found a 17% higher all-cause mortality risk per 10 beats per minute increase, and life-course cohort data also linked persistently elevated resting heart rate with higher mortality in later adulthood.
edges.population: community-dwelling adults and older adults without restricting to any one disease cohort
edges.mechanism: A high resting heart rate can reflect sympathetic overactivity, lower cardiorespiratory fitness, inflammation, underlying disease burden, or reduced physiologic reserve. Even when it is partly a marker rather than a pure cause, it tends to sit in the same biologic corridor as higher long-term mortality risk.
edges.summary: This threshold is one of the clearest simple biomarker signals in the map. Once resting heart rate is consistently above about 80 beats per minute, all-cause mortality risk is reliably higher across large prospective datasets, making a harmful direction much more plausible than a neutral one.
edges.caveats: Resting heart rate is influenced by medications, fitness, thyroid status, acute illness, and measurement context, so one isolated reading should not be over-interpreted. The association is strong enough for risk stratification, but it does not mean lowering heart rate in every context will automatically lower mortality.

evidence.notes: Resting heart rate and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in the general population: a meta-analysis.

evidence.citation: Dagfinn Aune et al 2017 Nutr Metab Cardiovasc Dis
evidence.notes: Resting heart rate and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer, and all-cause mortality - A systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies.
